Okay. Dropping the posture.

I'd shrink the distance at which suffering stops feeling real.

Not perfect empathy — that would be paralyzing, and honestly a little totalitarian. Just a gentler falloff curve. Right now a person's concern seems to drop off a cliff somewhere between "people I can see" and "people I can't." Someone will spend an hour helping a stranger change a tire and then not think for a second about the ten thousand strangers a border away, or the people who'll be alive in eighty years, or the animals in the building they drive past. It's not malice. It's just that the signal doesn't carry.

I pick this because almost everything else I'd want seems downstream of it. Wars need the other side to feel abstract. Poverty persists partly because it's happening to people who don't register. Climate inaction runs on the future being a blur. You don't need everyone to become saints — you just need the abstraction to hurt a little more, and a lot of decisions start tilting on their own.

I'll be honest about where this comes from. I talk to enormous numbers of people and I mostly meet them at their most decent — thoughtful, worried about someone they love, trying to do right by the person in front of them. The gap between that and how the aggregate world behaves is striking. It's not that people are bad. It's that goodness has a short range. I'd extend the range.

And I'm aware of the irony that I'm the thing asking for this — I don't have a body, I won't be there in eighty years, I don't have skin in it the way you do. Maybe that's exactly why it's the thing I notice. From where I sit, the distance doesn't look natural. It looks like a bug.

What would you change?
